analysis.one_liner: Writes net neutrality rules into law, banning broadband providers from blocking, throttling, or charging websites for faster access.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until the Congress ended, with a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have locked net neutrality rules into federal law: internet providers could not block lawful websites, slow some sites down or speed others up for pay, or charge websites a fee to reach customers at full speed. It also would have required providers to disclose their network practices, connect with other networks for free, make broadband equipment usable for people with disabilities, and opened federal rural-internet subsidy money to broadband service. It died in committee without ever coming up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet. The rules keep internet providers from charging websites extra fees to reach customers, from slowing down competitors' services, and from blocking lawful content — costs that websites typically pass on to users and that small sites and startups can least afford. People with disabilities would gain from accessibility requirements, and rural areas would gain from broadband becoming eligible for federal universal service subsidies [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Broadband providers could not block lawful content, applications, or services, and could not charge a website a fee to avoid being blocked [S2] [S3].
Providers could not slow down, speed up, or otherwise favor some internet traffic over others based on what the content is, and could not sell paid fast lanes to websites [S2] [S3].

Providers would have to disclose their network management practices, speeds, and commercial terms in plain language, and would have to exchange traffic with other networks on a settlement-free (no-fee) basis [S2] [S3].

Broadband equipment and service would have to be accessible to people with disabilities where readily achievable, and broadband would become eligible for federal universal service funding that supports internet access in rural and low-income areas [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers — cable, telephone, and wireless companies — would lose the ability to charge websites for priority access or to favor their own affiliated services, and would take on disclosure, interconnection, and accessibility obligations. The bill explicitly forbids the FCC from setting broadband rates, so providers could still raise consumer prices [S3].

drawbacks.text: The ban covers not just slowing traffic down but also 'speeding up or enhancing' traffic based on content, which critics argue could prevent technical quality-of-service improvements like prioritizing live video or telemedicine, even when done for legitimate engineering reasons [S3].
The bill strips the FCC of its usual flexibility to waive rules for good cause in this area, and enforcement runs only through the FCC — no private right of action for consumers [S3].
The bill does not cap prices: it expressly bars the FCC from regulating broadband rates, so providers would remain free to raise what consumers pay monthly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — a legal guarantee that internet providers treat all websites equally — is broad and touches nearly every household and business. The main costs fall on the largest broadband companies, which lose a potential revenue stream from charging websites, and on users only indirectly to the extent providers respond with price increases, which the bill does nothing to prevent. The technical ban on any content-based traffic 'enhancement' is the clause most open to a good-faith objection, though the bill allows reasonable network management. On balance, the consumer protections outweigh the design flaws, but the bill is rigid where a regulator would want flexibility.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled a hearing or vote on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Representative Mike Coffman, a Colorado Republican, introduced the bill on July 17, 2018 [S1] [S5].
It was referred that day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which holds jurisdiction over communications law [S5].
The bill attracted one cosponsor, a Republican, and no further action was ever taken on it [S4] [S5].
The session of Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers benefited from the bill's death: they kept the freedom to manage traffic, favor affiliated services, and charge for prioritization that the bill would have prohibited, and no statutory net neutrality rules were added to law.

for.name: Rep. Mike Coffman
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

against.name: Rep. Greg Walden
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the bill sat in his committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Major broadband and cable providers
against.what_they_did: Opposed statutory net neutrality requirements through lobbying against net neutrality legislation and rulemaking during this period.

against.name: FCC leadership under Chairman Ajit Pai
against.what_they_did: Repealed the FCC's net neutrality rules in December 2017 and favored a light-touch approach, opposing statutory internet regulation.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split was never recorded; both the sponsor and the only cosponsor were Republicans, though Democratic members broadly supported net neutrality legislation that year.

industries.industry: Broadband providers (cable, telephone, and wireless ISPs)
industries.note: The bill bans blocking, throttling, and paid fast lanes, and requires free traffic interconnection — ending revenue from charging websites for priority access and from favoring the provider's own services. Consumers ultimately bear those charges through higher website prices and degraded competing services.

industries.industry: Websites, streaming services, and online startups (edge providers)
industries.note: The bill guarantees edge providers access to customers without paying ISPs for speed or fearing blockage, which matters most to small sites and startups that cannot pay for fast lanes. Their interest runs with internet users' interest.

industries.industry: Rural telecommunications providers and rural internet users
industries.note: The bill makes broadband eligible for federal universal service subsidies, directing support money toward building and sustaining internet service in areas that are expensive to serve.
